spec: No entrance at all: every word and control is final at first paint, nothing fades or moves. Keep one ambient object running, such as a live counter, a drifting gradient or a film. Reading starts in under 0.5s, so the page feels fast and sure of itself.

Whole page appears in its final position at 25-65% ink and reaches full ink within 0.4-1s, with no translate, stagger or scale. Opacity 0.3-0.4s on cubic-bezier(.25,0,.5,1). Reads like a print developing, and it is the quietest entrance that still marks arrival.

Nav, headline and buttons paint at once; the media slot is already reserved at its exact size. Media fades in by about 1-2s with opacity 0.3s cubic-bezier(0,0,.2,1), no slide, no layout shift. Copy never waits for the heavy asset and never moves.

Reserve the hero with a flat plate sampled from the footage's first frame, at the exact size of the video, with nav and headline already placed on it. Fade the media up over 0.8-1.5s on its ready event, not a timer. No spinner, no shift, so a slow connection still looks designed.

Skeleton copies the final geometry exactly: same tile sizes, radii and caption bars in a flat 4-8% grey, with logo and primary controls live at once. Content swaps in tile by tile by about 2s with no reflow and no shimmer sweep. Best for feeds and catalogues.

Nav is solid from frame one. Headline fades from near zero with 8px blur, line by line, then subhead, then product, each about 1.3s on a gentle cubic-bezier(.4,0,.2,1), starts 0.2-0.5s apart, no travel. Readable by about 1.9s, done by 3s. Sharp out-curves make this pop.

Headline words resolve left to right from 10px blur through a saturated tint of the accent to sharp ink, about 0.75s each with a 140ms stagger, no translate. Subline follows, media last. Complete by about 2s. Use on headlines of seven words or fewer.

Headline lines or words rise 6-12px and fade with a 60-100ms stagger, cubic-bezier(.22,1,.36,1), 0.6-1.1s, while chip and buttons are already in place. A colour field or gradient blooms after the words land. Small travel is the whole difference from a default fade-up.

Copy and backdrop are present first. By 1-2s the product window rises 12-60px from below the fold edge with a fade, cubic-bezier(.22,1,.36,1), 0.7-1s, covering part of the backdrop. A small detail arrives last, such as a chat prompt or live counter. Conversion UI is never delayed.

Copy is static while the product assembles in 3-5 separate beats over 2-6s: card fades in, phone rises 8px through it, a banner lands last, or a status dot turns amber and an alert appears. Each beat is one thing, so the load plays the product's real job.

Headline and buttons are static from first paint. One owned object performs for 2-4s: a pixel glyph draws along its outline, a signal travels a connector, a wordmark rises behind a roofline. Nothing else moves, so the load feels authored and costs almost nothing to run.

Type and layout are final first. Then only light changes: a render rises from a 25% pastel ghost to full saturation in about 1s, or a glow blooms in a corner over 2-3s, with no slide or scale. The page feels lit rather than loaded.

One word in the headline loops through 3-4 products or audiences every 2-4s while the rest of the line holds. Swap with a short fade, 8px blur or retype, 200-300ms, and animate the width so the line re-centres smoothly. It is the only motion in the hero.

No preloader. The hero runs at once and swaps media in place while type stays locked: split halves change on their own beats about 1s apart, or one interior holds 5s then crossfades over 1.5s. No zoom, pan or parallax. The cut rhythm is the entire effect.

One headline line types character by character at 25-45ms a character with a thin caret, after the rest of the hero is already placed, or as the very last beat. Reserve the full line width first so nothing reflows. It makes the headline the event, so use it once.

Images arrive smaller, denser and rotated about 3-8 degrees, then spread and straighten over 1.5-3s with cubic-bezier(.16,1,.3,1) while headline words rise. Stagger 90-140ms from the centre outward. Best where the product is a collection of objects, and the end state must be a real layout.

Hero photo starts at 24-40px blur over a colour sampled from it and sharpens over 1-2s, cubic-bezier(.16,1,.3,1), while copy is already readable or fades in with it. Works like a lens racking, and it makes a slow image load look deliberate.

Flat brand colour fills the screen with one small centred mark, 40-100px, no spinner. Mark fades in within 0.5s, holds about 1s, then the page cuts or crossfades in. Under 1.5s in total. Reads as a hotel or house arriving, and it must appear on first visit only.

A real progress counter set large, 120-180px tabular numerals bottom-left, or 14px between two hairlines. It runs 0 to 100 tied to actual loading, usually 1-2s, while stills or a mark work beside it, then hands straight into the hero. A count that takes 5s is a tax.

The logo does something only this brand would do: a monogram writes itself stroke by stroke, a clock's hands sweep to the real time, a character walks in. 1.5-3s on flat ground, no bar or percent, then dissolve to the page. Spend it on brands with an owned mark.

Wordmark centred on a flat screen holds about 1s, then a single element travels and shrinks into its nav slot over 0.8-1.2s on cubic-bezier(.76,0,.24,1) while the panel behind lifts away. The page is already in place underneath. Use FLIP so one object makes the whole trip.

A film title card: blank ground 0.5s, a huge two-line statement or wordmark at 110-120px holds about 1.5-2s with no movement, then a hard cut or plain swap to the page. No fade, no bar. The confidence comes from the stillness and the cut.

A shape opens the page: a centred ring parts, a thumbnail or video tile grows to full bleed, a white stadium expands into the page sheet. 1-1.5s on cubic-bezier(.76,0,.24,1), clip-path or FLIP rather than width, and the shape must come from the brand.

Letters or a logo resolve through stepped states: glyph swaps settling left to right, or block mosaics halving in size. Use steps(), never a smooth tween, 30-60ms a step, 1-2s in total. Lock the text box first so nothing reflows. Suits technical and mono brands only.

A 4-6s scripted opening that plays before any scroll, like a keynote reveal: a case opens, an x-ray resolves into the render, parts slide together. Camera held, one idea, a skip affordance, and first visit only. Reserve it for launches where the object is the whole page.

Statement of 34-72px starts at 15-20% ink. Each word or character reaches full ink tied to scroll position, never to time, with a soft front 1-2 characters wide or a gradient spread over about 3 lines at reading height. Pace follows the reader. One per page, or one per chapter.

Whole lines or paragraphs wait at 15-60% ink and reach full ink one at a time as they near mid-viewport. Opacity or colour only, no translate, no split. Large type stays perfectly still, which is why it feels calmer than a rise. Use for stat stacks and short statements.

A heading resolves left to right behind a moving front: settled letters solid, a short gradient-coloured band at the front, then blurred pale letters ahead, with a second line waiting blurred below. Tie it to scroll. Body copy stays static. Spend it on one heading per section at most.

Copy enters from 8-12px blur and 30% opacity to sharp as it reaches the viewport, 0.4s cubic-bezier(.22,1,.36,1), with no translate. Softer than a rise, and it fits fashion, agency and premium brands. Keep it to display lines, because blurred small text reads as a rendering bug.

Items fade in where they stand with no offset: opacity 0.5s cubic-bezier(.25,1,.5,1), caught at unequal opacity as they pass. No translate, scale or parallax. The most respectful reveal, and it suits catalogues and documentation where layout must never appear to move under the reader.

A row enters left to right: each item 40-80ms after the last, 8-12px lower, about 0.3-0.5s, cubic-bezier(.25,.1,.3,1) or (.16,1,.3,1). The stagger belongs inside the row, not across the page. Runs once, stays small, and only on peers that should read as a set.

Rows brighten as they reach mid-viewport and dim as they leave, so one item is always in focus and the rest hold at about 35%. Transition 0.3-0.5s on opacity. Works for process lists, CVs and timelines. Keep a readable floor, since dimmed rows must still be legible.

Only small marginal objects move: stickers, cut-outs or line art drift at a different rate from the text, 20-80px over the viewport, and fade in near their heading. Panels and type stay still. CSS scroll timelines are enough. Motion lives in the margins, so reading is never disturbed.

Small mono labels enter as random glyphs resolving left to right, or thumbnails enter as a coarse block mosaic. Stepped, 300-600ms, on labels only, with body copy fading normally. Reads as a data read-out. Never decode anything longer than about four words.

1px lines travel along the page grid as you scroll, branching around headings and ending at nodes, with sections fading in behind them. stroke-dashoffset tied to scroll. It links separate sections into one circuit. Keep lines behind the type and on the grid.

Media does the entrance while text stays still: a video anchored to the right margin grows leftward from about 80% to full width, or a product rises from beneath with its screen state changing. 0.78s cubic-bezier(.22,1,.36,1). Anchor to one edge so the movement has a direction.

Cards pin under a sticky heading; each new card slides over the last, about 50px lower, widths stepping up (1138, 1260, 1320) so depth reads. Cards are translucent with backdrop-filter blur 22px, so covered copy softens where it passes under. Plain position:sticky, three to five cards.

The most useful pin on the web: plan names, prices and CTAs stick under the nav across thousands of pixels of table, and the section title pins until the next replaces it. Rows pass beneath with a hairline and no shadow. position:sticky only, no scroll listeners.

A slim position cue in the page chrome: a 2-3px top line growing with progress under a chapter nav, a 4px tick riding a rail edge, or a dark pill with a playhead. Active chapter updates per section. Use on long pages only, and replace a sticky header rather than add to one.

Panel pins for one screen per step. A left list activates the next item with a 1px rule and full ink, the rest at 40%; the pinned visual on the right swaps or re-lights to match, others dropping to 10%. Three to five steps, and each must also work as a plain stacked list on a phone.

One full-height frame pins while photographs cross-dissolve at the same framing, with a 12px caption block holding bottom-left. Nothing slides. Chapters change by dissolve rather than by page movement, so a long story reads as a slow film. Three to five stills of matching exposure.

A contained window pins and scales with scroll, about 750px wide to 2x, until it crops at the panel edge and UI text reads huge. Set transform-origin on the focal point, stop the scrub about a quarter early so the end holds, and avoid will-change, which blurs text.

Pinned scene where a small rectangle inside the image scales up to become the next image, about 0.3 viewports per step, three or four steps deep. It reads as falling through pictures. Needs images composed for it, with the next frame's edge exactly on the inner rectangle.

The hero does not scroll away. It pins, then either blurs about 40px and washes pale while centred paragraphs sit over it, or the product scales down to about 30% as the next panel lifts. The image becomes a backdrop instead of leaving, so the first chapter carries into the second.

One logo element travels with scroll from a large hero position to the header, for example 686px to 195px or 30px to 15px, scrubbed. The header stays empty until it arrives, so the brand appears once per screen. Scale with transform and align both ends to the same axis.

Vertical scroll drives a sideways pan across 5-10 items while title and index stay fixed and swap as each item reaches focus. Settle 0.7s cubic-bezier(.22,1,.36,1). Show the next item's edge at all times. Give it a vertical fallback on phones and never trap the wheel without a way out.

Page background, type, rules and nav interpolate together between sections, for example paper to near-black over about half a viewport, with the CTA staying bright above the shift. No wipe and no edge. The colour change is the transition, so the page acts as one surface.

The section argues by scrub: pinned, a scattered collage of the old way (receipts, forms, emails with dashed links) fades to pale wireframe as the heading swaps and one clean window remains. Or a scene flips to wireframe for a data chapter. Motion carries the claim itself.

One pinned 3D subject or layered diagram is scrubbed apart: lid, board and base separate about 250px along dotted guides, or panes fan in perspective. Ground steps tone between chapters, and only copy and the object change. Prerender frames or use a real model. Worth it only for a physical product.

A 1-1.5px line runs down the page and draws with scroll: ahead of the reader it sits at 20% opacity, the drawn portion at full ink. Rounded 20px elbows, nodes at each stop. It passes over type and illustration, and turns the whole page into one route.

One object stays on screen across several sections and changes as you scroll: a mark rotates 20 then 45 degrees, a phone swaps its screen, a model re-skins per project. Copy passes beside it. One object carries the story, so sections stop restarting.

Scroll or arrow keys fly a real camera between scenes in WebGL, with a tick ruler sliding under a fixed needle and a progress count such as 00/08. Needs a fixed-height page, keyboard control and a static fallback. Reserve it for portfolios and launch pages with no conversion job.

Layering links two sections with no fade: a large heading holds still while a 400-580px video card scrolls across it, lifted by one wide shadow, about 0 24px 60px at 20%. Keep the fixed layer legible when covered, and let the top layer exit under the nav.

Replace a hard section edge with a 100-180px band of 12px tiles on a 1px grid, ramping dark through grey to light, top rows randomly missing. Reverse it at the far end of the section. Static or scrubbed, it costs nothing, and the page gets an owned seam.

Wheel input drives a stage instead of the page: the first input fills a CTA and shows a 12px hint, a photo scales 1.08 while letters bend along a curve, or a sentence flies along a path. One screen tall, with visible progress and every key working. Expressive sites only.

Every control moves one step on its own scale: fill changes about 10 L*, dark fills lighten, light and mid fills darken. background-color only, 0.15s cubic-bezier(.4,0,.2,1), no transform, no shadow. The default of Vercel, Grafana and Exa. It reads as a system, not an effect.

Nav items and rows gain a pill of 4-8% ink with the text stepping to full ink, 0.1-0.2s, no movement. On photos or dark grounds use white at 8-20% instead. The chip fills a target the eye can land on, without inventing any new colour.

The control recedes: opacity or alpha falls to 0.75-0.9 on buttons and 0.5-0.7 on links, 0.1-0.2s, with nothing else changing. One rule for every colour, so a page with many brand fills needs no hover palette. Polar and Nuxt run whole systems on it.

The button dims to opacity 0.6 and a hidden arrow stem fades from 0 to 1 beside its chevron, 0.15s cubic-bezier(.215,.61,.355,1), with the fill unchanged. A chevron extending into an arrow says go without moving the box. Stripe's signature, and it needs an SVG with a separate stem path.

On dark UI text, border and surface all step up together, one notch each: grey text to white, border +10 levels, surface +5 to +7, 0.1-0.2s. Never darken on dark, and use no shadow. Linear uses filter brightness(1.03) on cards and brightness(1.3) on links.

The fill jumps to a second brand colour instead of a shade: accent to ink, or black to a pale mint with a dark label. 0.15-0.3s. Border and label move with it. This is loud, so keep it to the one or two actions that matter and give the rest a quieter hover.

Fill and label swap exactly, and the outline button fills: white on ink becomes ink on white. 0.15-0.3s on colour, background and border together. Binary and flat, no lift. Best in mono or two-colour systems, where a third tone would break the logic.

Zero transition on purpose: colour, fill or underline change in one frame. A hard cut reads as fast and printed, like a switch. It suits type-led, editorial and brutalist sites, and it needs one sharp value change, because a 3% tone step with no easing just looks broken.

Links answer with an underline and nothing else: 1px, offset 2-4px, usually in 0s. A drawn version scales from scaleX(0) to 1 in 0.3s cubic-bezier(0,0,.2,1), origin left on enter and right on leave. Keep it on words, because that is the oldest signal the web has.

The page rests in neutrals and every control resolves to one accent on hover: links, titles and rows go ink to accent in 0.15s, and the main CTA fills. The accent appears only under the pointer, so the colour feels earned and the system needs no extra tokens.

Only the arrow moves: +2 to +6px in x, 0.2-0.3s cubic-bezier(.25,1,.5,1), while the fill takes a quiet tone step. Baseten runs it diagonally at (5px,-5px) for up-right arrows. The box stays put, so it gives direction without the page feeling jumpy.

Two stacked labels clipped to one line box, never to the button: the first translates up by its line height, the copy rises from below. 0.32-0.46s cubic-bezier(.22,1,.36,1). Fill stays unchanged. Precise and mechanical, like a departures board. Hide the copy from screen readers.

A fill layer sweeps in from one side instead of fading: span scaleX 0 to 1 or translateY from just outside the box, 0.3-0.5s cubic-bezier(.4,0,.2,1), label colour following. Set the origin to the entry side so it leaves the way it came. Has a clear direction and a little theatre.

The button rises 1-2px with a two-layer shadow tinted by the brand, alpha about 10% and 16%, 0.2-0.3s cubic-bezier(.25,1,.5,1). Cards lift at most 4px. Measured median lift is 2px on main buttons and 1px on cards, so anything you can clearly see travel is too much.

The button jumps +4px x, -4px y while a solid shadow appears at -4px 4px 0, or a pale plate sits under it and the face moves (-8px,-8px). 0.15s linear or 0.28s cubic-bezier(.215,.61,.355,1). Printed, sticker-like and physical, and it needs a matching system of hard edges.

The button does not move. Its ring thickens from 1px to 2px with box-shadow 0 0 0, and the label steps to full ink, 0.1s ease-in-out. Slack thickens an inset ring over 0.42s. No layout shift, because box-shadow takes no space. Calm, tactile and easy to theme.

Scale only: 1.04-1.05 up on pills, or 0.98 down as a press. 0.15-0.2s, using the scale property so it composes with other transforms. Grows no more than 1-2px on any edge in spirit, and larger buttons take a smaller factor. Consumer and media brands wear it best.

An overshoot curve such as cubic-bezier(.34,1.56,.64,1) on something small: a label dot scales 0 to 1 in 0.5s, a logo tilts -8 degrees, a marker slides 4.5px past and back. Keep it under about 200px wide. Playful brands only, because overshoot on a card reads as a toy.

On dark, a soft light replaces movement: box-shadow none to 0 0 32px white at 50%, or 0 6px 16px accent at 12% with the border moving to 40% accent, 0.2s. Inngest fades in a 360px radial spotlight over 0.42s on cards. Spend it on one control, or nothing glows.

The image scales inside a fixed frame with overflow hidden: 1.02-1.05 for product and premium, 1.1 for consumer. Slower than the controls, 0.3-0.6s, and up to 1s on cubic-bezier(.23,1,.32,1). Apple uses 1.0161. The frame never moves, which is what keeps it dignified.

The card changes what it says rather than how high it sits: a second product image crossfades in over 0.4s, a tinted fill arrives with an underlined line, a typed suffix such as ' > SHOP' appears, or the poster grows 12px. No shadow and no lift.

An inverse highlight: the item under the pointer drops to 35-50% opacity over 0.3-0.4s cubic-bezier(.25,1,.5,1), with no scale or underline. The art keeps its framing, which suits galleries and magazines where the work must not be decorated.

The card stays where it is and only its 1px border darkens one step, for example #EBEBEB to #BDBDBD, 0.12-0.15s. No lift, shadow or scale. Hugging Face adds a faint fill and small corner ticks. It matches a document feel and keeps dense grids calm.

The whole row takes a fill edge to edge in about 0.2s, text following: a pale tint for tables and FAQs, solid ink with cream text for index lists, or text alone turning the accent. Rules and position stay still, and the row must be a single link.

The hovered row does something owned: grows 16px past both table edges with a pale fill and 12px radius, gains a hatched fill and hard offset, shows a 100px gradient segment on its rules, or reveals three thumbnails. 0.2s. Colour and detail appear only under the cursor.

Only the hovered row opens: height grows from about 19-177px to 240-460px, pushing later rows down while the others collapse into strips. 0.5s cubic-bezier(.25,1,.5,1). An index becomes a gallery. Needs a stable pointer path, so give a row no neighbour that jumps under the cursor.

The hovered row snaps to full ink while its neighbours fall to about 30%, and a small thumbnail tile appears in the indent. Use a CSS :has() rule or group hover. Attention moves by subtraction, so the list stays quiet at rest. Polar uses the same idea on menu rows.

A menu trigger's chevron rotates 180 degrees in 0.2-0.3s while the label takes a 5-8% tint. The colour may snap, but the rotation should ease, because the chevron carries the state. Rotate back on close. It is the one transform almost every product nav uses.

Most controls are deliberately inert. Only one kind responds, for example nav links or a single chip, and the hero film or demo holds the attention. Scale AI scales one inner span to 0.9. Across the sample half of cards, rows and text links do nothing at all.

One row of monochrome logos 24-40px high drifts in a centred 760-1200px window, both ends masked to transparent over 40-80px with mask-image. 40-60s per loop, linear. Pause on hover and under reduced motion. It says a long list without a wall of logos.

Logos near each edge blur progressively to unreadable and dim while the centre stays crisp, instead of an opacity mask. Stack three masked backdrop-filter layers at 1, 3 and 8px, with zones sized in percent so a phone keeps its centre. A lens-like focus for dark pages.

The ticker has no fade. It is clipped hard by the page rail or the panel radius, so items appear and vanish exactly at the drawn line. Monochrome logos about 30px high under a closing hairline. Works only where those lines are already the page's structure.

Two rows of 34-44px hairline chips drift in opposite directions inside a 640px window, masked at both ends, second row offset by half a chip. Shows a long integration list in a small space. Add a static line under it naming what the list means.

A full-bleed band 44-120px tall between sections, solid brand colour, 16-52px caps repeating with an owned glyph as separator. Doubles as a hard section seam. Best when the separator is a brand joke: Headspace uses googly eyes whose pupils aim differently in each instance.

One line at 96-145px of bold type runs edge to edge, cropped by both sides, usually the last loud moment before the footer. An asterisk or star separates phrases. Slow it to 30-40s per loop, and let the page's velocity nudge it if you want it to feel alive.

A one-line ticker of real numbers at the hero base: fixed 11px label on the left, scrolling caps labels with tabular values in chips, split by 1px ticks, right edge fading. Values climb live. Proof instead of decoration, and it must use real or honestly labelled data.

Long lists run as texture behind a card or cutout: two to eight rows of 20px text at 20-60% ink, drifting, offset, with a 12px PAUSE MOTION control below. It shows scale without asking anyone to read it. The foreground object must stay fully legible.

Rows of images or video drift across the full width: 224-342px tiles, 16-24px gaps, 60-90s per loop, one to three rows offset, edges washed to the page colour. Include a visible pause control on any video. It softens uneven customer photos into one texture.

A fixed ~44px band at the viewport bottom whose text and fill change with the current slide or section, so it doubles as a progress signal. Or caption-style lines that swap every 3s. It holds state, so it earns its permanent place.

A real DOM card plays a 6-10s script with a drawn cursor: it types in a field, a tick appears, a button presses, a result card slides out. Live UI, not video, so text stays crisp. Animate x and y on separate curves so the path arcs, dip scale on click, hold 2s at the end.

Tabs auto-advance every 5-8s, and a 2-3px line grows along the active tab as a visible timer, then the next takes over. Hover pauses, click takes control and stops the cycle. The timer tells people that the change is deliberate and when it will come.

The hero window types a real prompt or command in bursts, about 40-85ms a character with a 150-240ms beat at each space, then output arrives row by row and older rows dim to 40%. 6-8s per loop, 2s hold on the result. Hover pauses. Proves the claim before any scroll.

Feature cards run small truths in place: figures tick, a bar fills, a checklist advances with spinner then tick, a chart extends and its tag flips. Mono text, loops under 8s. Motion stays inside the UI and the page frame stays still.

The camera does the storytelling: the demo opens zoomed hard into a prompt at about 100px type, then pulls back to the whole builder, or a full window pushes in 3x until one button fills the panel. Attention lands exactly where the claim is. Use for one hero only.

Autoplaying muted clips inside tiles, cutting every 2-3s, with the layout around them still. Use a poster frame, 2-8MB per clip, lazy loading, and a pause control. A synthetic cursor inside the footage performs the action. Cheap to make and easy to keep honest.

The product is drawn as a diagram that runs: packets pass through a band, cards change state at a scan line, or speech flows along a ribbon into a capsule and leaves polished. Confined to one band under the nav, so it never competes with the headline.

Coloured cursors with ~12px name flags drift across a live canvas and act on real objects, while a caret edits a label. Square-cornered tags, three people at most. It shows collaboration as a behaviour, and it makes an empty page feel inhabited.

A small loop drawn in characters or pixels, with no video: an ASCII figure flips between frames, pixels swap on the logo's own grid, a chalk outline jitters between marks. Stepped timing, 6-12 fps. Tiny to ship, and it reads as made by hand.

The control for a loop, drawn small: 2px segments with the current one filling as a timer, a 6px vertical dash stack, or a translucent 110x32 pause pill bottom left. It replaces dots and arrows, and it is also how a looping hero stays accessible.

Over project media a small tag trails the pointer about 15px down-right: 40-94px wide, 10-13px label such as VIEW, lerp about 0.15 per frame. Stays small so the work stays the subject. It replaces the card's button, so the whole tile is the target. Keep the system cursor visible.

Over a rail the pointer gains a 120px flat disc in a pale brand colour with 14px/700 DRAG centred. It is an instruction, so it appears only where the gesture works and scales in from 0.6 in 0.25s. One disc grammar across WATCH and DRAG.

The arrow is replaced with a 12-20px solid dot or square, sometimes flipping colour over dark slabs. No trail, no lag. It costs a little usability, because small targets lose their hotspot. Portfolios only, and leave text fields and all touch devices alone.

A 70-108px object has its own physics rather than following the mouse: scroll throws a solid circle down the viewport and stretches it into a tilted ellipse along velocity, and it recovers round at rest. Never covers controls for long, and it is switched off under reduced motion.

A custom 20-36px arrow or emoji replaces the system cursor, or coloured arrow cursors sit in the page to suggest a live canvas. Trivial to build with the CSS cursor property. Only a very playful brand survives it, and it must fall back to the system cursor.

The page answers the pointer, not the cursor: when it enters a rail the headline blurs about 8px and drops to 20% so the rail takes over, and it returns when focus leaves. Eased over 0.3s. It moves attention, and it needs no custom cursor at all.

A full-screen brand-colour panel wipes across between pages, 0.8-1s on cubic-bezier(.86,0,.07,1), with a centred line or logo at the midpoint. Swap the route while covered. Under 1s in total, and skip it entirely for repeat navigation and under reduced motion.

Name and image are masked by about 10 vertical bars staggering across the width, about 1.4s, cubic-bezier(.23,1,.32,1). The outgoing title stays legible in the gaps while the next one builds. Rich, precise and tied to product launches. Bars should echo a real edge in the product.

The frame never moves. Title and still cross-swap in the same position, so only image and words change. Duration 0.3-0.6s. The quietest transition that still feels authored, because the layout itself is the constant.

A small outlined toggle reskins the page in a wipe, ground and type changing together while a duplicate nav slides in under the old one. A mood switch in place of a dark-mode toggle. Works as a brand gesture on a portfolio.

Between dark shots the film flips to a near-white, silver, negative-like exposure at about 36%, then returns to black. A shutter flash that separates chapters. It must be fast and rare, and it must respect photosensitivity, so never repeat it within a second.

A solid disc scales on the ground and covers the screen before the next scene appears, about 1s. Use clip-path circle() so it stays crisp. Starts from the click point if it can, because a transition that begins where the person acted feels caused rather than scheduled.
